title: What a short run tells you
objectives: Use short runs to debug training: overfit one batch and sweep the learning rate.

screens.title: Three runs
screens.prose: Three runs of 10 steps from the same small random weights. One has a bug that stops the gradients reaching the weights; one has too high a learning rate; one is healthy.
screens.question: Which run has the bug?

options.text: A, flat at its first value
B, which jumps about
options.why: B moves, so gradients reach the weights; its steps are too big.

options.text: C, which falls steadily
options.why: C is the healthy run.

hints.text: A bug that blocks gradients leaves the weights unchanged.
Unchanged weights give the same loss every step... on the same batch.
Look for a curve that never moves.

feedback.correct: A never moves: the weights did not change, so no gradient reached them.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which run shows no learning at all?

explain.text: A is flat, B jumps as high as 6.91 (rate 0.1) and C falls to 3.24 (rate 0.01). Ten steps already separate the three.

screens.title: A learning-rate sweep
screens.prose: The same 10 steps at seven learning rates, from small random weights, on the same batches. Slide through the rates.
screens.question: Which rate gives the lowest loss at step 10?

options.why: At 0.1 the loss jumps about and ends at 3.568.
At 0.0001 the loss barely moves: 4.136.
At 0.03 the loss ends at 3.375, above 0.01's.

hints.text: Read the last loss in each caption.
The smallest is the winner.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the last losses in the captions.

explain.text: Too small a rate barely moves; too large overshoots. Over 10 steps 0.01 does best here, 3.236; the long run used 0.003 with warm-up and decay, safer over 5,000 steps.

screens.title: The loss at step 0
screens.prose: Before any step, a model with small random weights should score about $\ln 65 \approx 4.1744$. A colleague's run starts at 5.9.
screens.question: What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Initial weights that are too large
The learning rate is too high
options.why: Step 0 comes before any update, so the rate cannot affect it.

options.text: The validation text is unusual
options.why: Any text scores about $\ln 65$ under a uniform guess.

options.text: Nothing: higher is better at the start
options.why: Lower loss is always better; 5.9 is worse than guessing uniformly.

hints.text: What does the loss at step 0 depend on?
Only the starting weights.
Large logits give confident guesses, often wrong.

feedback.correct: Above $\ln 65$ at step 0 means confident wrong guesses: large initial weights.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Step 0 depends only on the starting weights.

explain.text: A loss above $\ln V$ before training means the logits are large. Shrink the initial weights, as l6 did with 0.02, before tuning anything else.

screens.title: Loss after 10 steps against the rate
screens.prose: Plotting the loss at step 10 against the learning rate on a log axis gives the sweep at a glance.
screens.question: The rate 0.1 ends lower than 0.0001. Does that make 0.1 a good rate?

options.text: No: its loss jumped above 6.9 on the way, so it is unstable
Yes: a lower final loss is all that matters
options.why: One noisy batch at step 10 hides the spike to 6.91. An unstable run often blows up later.

options.text: Yes, and higher still would be better
options.why: Past the best rate the loss rises again; that is the shape of the sweep.

options.text: No rate can be judged in 10 steps
options.why: Ten steps cannot pick the final rate, but they do show which rates are unstable.

hints.text: Look at the whole run at 0.1, not only step 10.
It reached 6.91.
An unstable rate is too high whatever its last value.

feedback.correct: Rate 0.1 spiked to 6.91: too high, even though its step 10 looks fine.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Look at how the run got there.

explain.text: A sweep picks the largest rate that still falls smoothly; here that is about 0.01. Beyond it the curve turns up and the runs grow erratic.

screens.title: Overfit one batch
screens.prose: A model that can learn should drive the loss on **one fixed batch** towards 0: it has 18,017 numbers to memorise 128 next characters. Here are 100 Adam steps on 4 windows at two rates.
screens.question: What does a run like this check?

options.text: That the whole loop can fit data at all
That the model generalises to new text
options.why: One batch says nothing about new text; it only shows the machinery works.

options.text: Which rate to use for the long run
options.why: Memorising one batch favours large rates that may be unstable on fresh batches.

options.text: That training is finished already
options.why: It memorised 4 windows; the real run has 225,000 characters to learn.

hints.text: What would stop a correct model memorising 128 characters?
Nothing, given enough steps.
Failing to do it points to a bug.

feedback.correct: At rate 0.01 the batch loss falls to 0.0015: the forward pass, backward pass and step all work.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What can you learn from memorising one batch?

explain.text: Overfitting one batch is the cheapest end-to-end test: rate 0.01 reaches 0.0015 in 100 steps. A loss stuck well above 0 here means the gradients or the update are broken.

screens.title: Write the overfit test
screens.prose: Write `overfit_one_batch(steps, lr, seed)`: start from `init_weights(seed)` and take `steps` Adam steps on the fixed batch `XO`, `YO` (4 windows of 32) with `loss_and_grads` and `adam_update`. Return the batch losses.
screens.question: Write `overfit_one_batch`.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np
from gpt_ops_l3 import init_weights, loss_and_grads, adam_init, adam_update


def overfit_one_batch(steps, lr, seed):
    # Start from init_weights(seed). Train on the one fixed batch XO, YO (defined for you) for `steps`
    # Adam steps at rate lr, using loss_and_grads and adam_update. Return the list of batch losses.
    ...
widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from gpt_ops_l3 import init_weights, loss_and_grads, adam_init, adam_update


def overfit_one_batch(steps, lr, seed):
    w = init_weights(seed)
    state = adam_init(w)
    losses = []
    for _ in range(steps):
        loss, grads = loss_and_grads(w, XO, YO)
        w = adam_update(w, grads, state, lr)
        losses.append(loss)
    return losses

widget.how: Submit runs 4 hidden tests. Test 1 compares the first 3 losses at rate 0.01 to $10^{-6}$ (relative). Tests 2 and 3 run 100 steps for seeds 0 and 1 and need the last loss below 0.01, a few seconds each. Test 4 checks the length at rate 0.

mutants.source:
import numpy as np
from gpt_ops_l3 import init_weights, loss_and_grads, adam_init, adam_update


def overfit_one_batch(steps, lr, seed):
    w = init_weights(seed)
    state = adam_init(w)
    losses = []
    for _ in range(steps):
        X, Y = _gb(np.array(_G.encode(open('tiny-shakespeare.txt').read()[:225000])), 4, 32, np.random.default_rng(len(losses)))
        loss, grads = loss_and_grads(w, X, Y)
        w = adam_update(w, grads, state, lr)
        losses.append(loss)
    return losses
mutants.symptom: Draws a fresh batch every step, so it is not overfitting one batch.

def overfit_one_batch(steps, lr, seed):
    w = init_weights(seed)

hints.text: Make the Adam state once, before the loop.
Each step: `loss, grads = loss_and_grads(w, XO, YO)`, then `w = adam_update(w, grads, state, lr)`.
Append each loss.

feedback.correct: Your run memorises the batch: the reference ends at 0.0015.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 compares the first three losses: same batch every step, one Adam state, keep the new weights.

explain.text: Same batch, one optimiser state, new weights each step. If this cannot reach near 0, nothing longer will work.

screens.title: Judged by the training loss
screens.prose: A colleague reports a loss of 0.0015 nats a character after 100 steps, and calls the model the best they have trained. It is the overfit run.
screens.question: What does that model score on the validation text?

options.text: About 8.04, worse than a uniform guess
About 0.0015, the same as on its batch
options.why: It memorised 128 characters; new text is not those characters.

options.text: About 2.46, like the bigram
options.why: It has seen too little text to learn even pair counts; its confident guesses are wrong.

options.text: About 1.79, like the supplied model
options.why: The supplied model trained on 5,000 batches, not one.

hints.text: It saw 4 windows, all memorised.
On new text it predicts those windows' characters with confidence.
Confident wrong guesses cost more than uniform ones.

feedback.correct: It scores 8.04 on validation: memorising one batch made it confidently wrong elsewhere.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What did it learn beyond those 4 windows?

byKey.same: That is the trap: a training loss says nothing about new text. Always report the held-out loss.

explain.text: Training loss 0.0015, validation 8.04, above $\ln 65 \approx 4.1744$. A training loss alone cannot rank models.

screens.title: A perfectly flat loss
screens.prose: A run on one fixed batch prints the same loss, 4.175866, at every step, to every digit.
screens.question: What does an exactly constant loss on a fixed batch tell you?

options.text: No update ever reached the weights
The rate is a little too small
options.why: A small rate still moves the loss in the later digits.

options.text: Training has fully converged
options.why: From random weights at 4.18, nothing has been learned yet.

options.text: The rate is much too high
options.why: Too high a rate makes the loss jump, not freeze.

hints.text: Same batch, same weights, same loss.
So the weights are the same.
Look for a rate of 0, or new weights that are never kept.

feedback.correct: Identical losses on one batch mean identical weights: the update is lost somewhere.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What must be true for every digit to repeat?

explain.text: Even a tiny rate changes the loss in some digit. An exact repeat means the step was never applied: a rate of 0, a dropped return value, or gradients that are all zero.

screens.title: Write the diagnosis
screens.prose: Write `diagnose(losses)` for a short run. It is `diverging` if any loss is not finite or is more than 10% above the first. It is `stuck` if every loss equals the first, and `slow` if the last is above 0.98 times the first. Otherwise it is `healthy`. `SWEEP` holds the seven 10-step runs.
screens.question: Write `diagnose`.

widget.how: Submit runs 8 hidden tests: the sweep at rates 0.01, 0.1, 0.0001 and 0.0003, a flat run, a run that reaches nan, a rising run and one that falls only 2%.

mutants.symptom: Looks only at the last loss, so a run that spiked and came back reads as healthy.
Misses nan, which compares false with everything.
Never calls a flat run stuck.

hints.text: Check `math.isfinite` on every loss first.
Compare `max(losses)` with `1.1 * losses[0]`.
Then flat, then slow, else healthy.

feedback.correct: Your rules sort every planted run correctly.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 is rate 0.1, which spikes above 6.9 and comes back. Look at the largest loss, not the last.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 reaches nan; `nan > x` is False, so test it with `math.isfinite`.

explain.text: The rules read the whole curve: a spike, a freeze, a crawl. Run them on every short run before trusting a long one.

screens.title: What a short run tells you
screens.question: A run passes the step-0 and one-batch checks but its sweep is flat at every rate. What is the next suspect?

options.text: The batches the sweep draws
The backward pass again
options.why: The one-batch check passed, so gradients and updates work.

options.text: The initial weights again
options.why: Step 0 was near $\ln V$, so the start is fine.

options.text: The choice of the seven rates
options.why: Seven rates over three orders of magnitude cover the useful range.

hints.text: Which part does the sweep use that the one-batch test does not?

feedback.correct: Only the sweep draws new batches each step: check the sampler and the targets.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which piece differs between the two checks?

explain.text: Each check isolates a part: step 0 the start, one batch the gradients, the sweep the data and the rate. Failing only the sweep points at the batches.

screens.title: A desk checklist
screens.prose: Karpathy's "A Recipe for Training Neural Networks" (2019) asks for these checks before any long run. A quant team adopts them for a new return-prediction net and wants one rule on the wall.
screens.question: Which order matches the recipe?

options.text: Step 0 loss, one batch, a rate sweep, then the long run
Train long first, then debug if the result is poor
options.why: A poor long run has many possible causes; short checks isolate them first.

options.text: Sweep rates first, then check the loss at step 0
options.why: Step 0 needs no training and catches a bad start before any sweep.

options.text: Watch only the validation loss throughout
options.why: Validation loss is the final judge, but it cannot tell a bug from a bad rate.

hints.text: Start with the check that costs nothing.
Then the one that tests the gradients.
Then tune.

feedback.correct: Cheapest and most specific first: step 0, one batch, a sweep, then the long run on held-out loss.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Order the checks from cheapest to most expensive.

explain.text: Each step rules out one class of failure before paying for the next. The same order debugs a return model, a CNN or the tiny GPT.

ideas: Step 0 should score about $\ln V$; one fixed batch should be memorised towards 0; a flat loss to every digit means no update reached the weights.
A 10-step sweep picks the largest rate that falls smoothly: 0.01 here (3.24 at step 10); 0.1 spiked to 6.91.
Judge runs by held-out loss: the memorised batch scored 0.0015 on itself and 8.04 on validation.
summary.trap: Ranking runs by training loss: memorising one batch looks perfect and generalises worse than guessing.

quiz.question: A character model with 96 symbols starts training at 4.57 nats. What does that say?

options.text: The start is fine: it is about $\ln 96$
The weights are too large
options.why: $\ln 96 \approx 4.56$, so 4.57 is a near-uniform start.

options.text: The rate is much too high
options.why: Step 0 comes before any update.

feedback.correct: $\ln 96 \approx 4.56$, the loss of a uniform guess: a good start.

explain.text: Small weights give about $\ln V$ at step 0; for $V = 96$ that is 4.56.

quiz.question: Every 10-step run in a sweep, at every rate, prints the same loss to every digit on the same batches. What is wrong?

options.text: The update never reaches the weights
All the rates are too small
options.why: A small rate still changes the later digits.

options.text: The initial weights are too small
options.why: Small weights still learn; the loss would move.

feedback.correct: Identical losses mean identical weights: the step is lost.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What makes every digit repeat?

explain.text: Look for a dropped return value, a rate of 0 or gradients that never reach the arrays.

quiz.question: A model memorises its training batch to 0.002 nats but scores 7.9 on validation. Which is true?

options.text: It overfits its batch
Its backward pass is wrong
options.why: A wrong backward pass could not memorise the batch.

options.text: The validation text is corrupt
options.why: A model trained on one batch is expected to do badly on new text.

feedback.correct: Memorising a batch proves the machinery works, not that the model generalises.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What does a low training loss alone show?

explain.text: Report the held-out loss. A training loss near 0 with a validation loss above $\ln V$ is memorisation.
